L44: # Working with Arrays of Strings And Bytes【26†#】
L45: 
L46: While NumPy is primarily a numerical library, it is often convenient to work with NumPy arrays of strings or bytes. The two most common use cases are:
L47: 
L48:   * Working with data loaded or memory-mapped from a data file, where one or more of the fields in the data is a string or bytestring, and the maximum length of the field is known ahead of time. This often is used for a name or label field.
L49:   * Using NumPy indexing and broadcasting with arrays of Python strings of unknown length, which may or may not have data defined for every value.
L50: For the first use case, NumPy provides the fixed-width 【27†`numpy.void`】, 【28†`numpy.str_`】 and 【29†`numpy.bytes_`】 data types. For the second use case, numpy provides 【30†`numpy.dtypes.StringDType`】. Below we describe how to work with both fixed-width and variable-width string arrays, how to convert between the two representations, and provide some advice for most efficiently working with string data in NumPy.
L51: ## Fixed-width data types【31†#】
L52: 
L53: Before NumPy 2.0, the fixed-width 【28†`numpy.str_`】, 【29†`numpy.bytes_`】, and 【27†`numpy.void`】 data types were the only types available for working with strings and bytestrings in NumPy. For this reason, they are used as the default dtype for strings and bytestrings, respectively:
L54: 
L55:     >>> np.array(["hello", "world"])
L56:     array(['hello', 'world'], dtype='<U5')
L57: Here the detected data type is `'<U5'`, or little-endian unicode string data, with a maximum length of 5 unicode code points.
L58: 
L59: Similarly for bytestrings:
L60: 
L61:     >>> np.array([b"hello", b"world"])
L62:     array([b'hello', b'world'], dtype='|S5')
L63: 
L64: 
L65: Since this stores individual bytes, the byteorder is ‘|’ (not applicable), and the data type detected is a maximum 5-byte bytestring.
L66: You can also use 【27†`numpy.void`】 to represent bytestrings:
L67: 
L68:     >>> np.array([b"hello", b"world"]).astype(np.void)
L69:     array([b'\x68\x65\x6C\x6C\x6F', b'\x77\x6F\x72\x6C\x64'], dtype='|V5')
L70: 
L71: 
L72: This is most useful when working with byte streams that are not well represented as bytestrings, and instead are better thought of as collections of 8-bit integers.
L73: ## Variable-width strings【32†#】
L74: 
L75: Added in version 2.0.
L76: 
L77: Note
L78: 
L79: 【30†`numpy.dtypes.StringDType`】 is a new addition to NumPy, implemented using the new support in NumPy for flexible user-defined data types and is not as extensively tested in production workflows as the older NumPy data types.
L80: Often, real-world string data does not have a predictable length. In these cases it is awkward to use fixed-width strings, since storing all the data without truncation requires knowing the length of the longest string one would like to store in the array before the array is created.
L81: To support situations like this, NumPy provides 【30†`numpy.dtypes.StringDType`】, which stores variable-width string data in a UTF-8 encoding in a NumPy array:
L82: 
L83:     >>> from numpy.dtypes import StringDType
L84:     >>> data = ["this is a longer string", "short string"]
L85:     >>> arr = np.array(data, dtype=StringDType())
L86:     >>> arr
L87:     array(['this is a longer string', 'short string'], dtype=StringDType())
L88: Note that unlike fixed-width strings, `StringDType` is not parameterized by the maximum length of an array element, arbitrarily long or short strings can live in the same array without needing to reserve storage for padding bytes in the short strings.
L89: Also note that unlike fixed-width strings and most other NumPy data types, `StringDType` does not always store the string data in the “main” `ndarray` data buffer. Instead, the array buffer can store short strings or metadata about where longer string data are stored in memory. This difference means that code expecting the array buffer to contain string data will not function correctly, and will need to be updated to support `StringDType`.
L90: ### Missing data support【33†#】
L91: 
L92: Often string datasets are not complete, and a special label is needed to indicate that a value is missing. By default `StringDType` does not have any special support for missing values, besides the fact that empty strings are used to populate empty arrays:
L93: 
L94:     >>> np.empty(3, dtype=StringDType())
L95:     array(['', '', ''], dtype=StringDType())
L96: Optionally, you can create an instance of `StringDType` with support for missing values by passing `na_object` as a keyword argument for the initializer:
L97: 
L98:     >>> dt = StringDType(na_object=None)
L99:     >>> arr = np.array(["this array has", None, "as an entry"], dtype=dt)
L100:     >>> arr
L101:     array(['this array has', None, 'as an entry'],
L102:           dtype=StringDType(na_object=None))
L103:     >>> arr[1] is None
L104:     True
L105: The `na_object` can be any arbitrary python object. Common choices are 【34†`numpy.nan`】, `float('nan')`, `None`, an object specifically intended to represent missing data like `pandas.NA`, or a (hopefully) unique string like `"__placeholder__"`.
L106: 
L107: NumPy has special handling for NaN-like sentinels and string sentinels.
L108: #### NaN-like Missing Data Sentinels【35†#】
L109: A NaN-like sentinel returns itself as the result of arithmetic operations. This includes the python `nan` float and the Pandas missing data sentinel `pd.NA`. NaN-like sentinels inherit these behaviors in string operations. This means that, for example, the result of addition with any other string is the sentinel:
L110: 
L111:     >>> dt = StringDType(na_object=np.nan)
L112:     >>> arr = np.array(["hello", np.nan, "world"], dtype=dt)
L113:     >>> arr + arr
L114:     array(['hellohello', nan, 'worldworld'], dtype=StringDType(na_object=nan))
L115: Following the behavior of `nan` in float arrays, NaN-like sentinels sort to the end of the array:
L116: 
L117:     >>> np.sort(arr)
L118:     array(['hello', 'world', nan], dtype=StringDType(na_object=nan))
L119: 
L120: 
L121: Comparisons also follow floating-point NaN semantics: equality and ordered comparisons involving a NaN-like sentinel return `False`, while inequality returns `True`.
L122: 
L123:     >>> arr != "hello"
L124:     array([False,  True,  True])
L125: #### String Missing Data Sentinels【36†#】
L126: 
L127: A string missing data value is an instance of `str` or subtype of `str`. If such an array is passed to a string operation or a cast, “missing” entries are treated as if they have a value given by the string sentinel. Comparison operations similarly use the sentinel value directly for missing entries.
L128: #### Other Sentinels【37†#】
L129: 
L130: Other objects, such as `None` are also supported as missing data sentinels. If any missing data are present in an array using such a sentinel, then operations such as sorting will raise an error:
L131: 
L132:     >>> dt = StringDType(na_object=None)
L133:     >>> arr = np.array(["this array has", None, "as an entry"], dtype=dt)
L134:     >>> np.sort(arr)
L135:     Traceback (most recent call last):
L136:     ...
L137:     ValueError: Cannot compare null that is not a nan-like value
L138: ### Coercing Non-strings【38†#】
L139: 
L140: By default, non-string data are coerced to strings:
L141: 
L142:     >>> np.array([1, object(), 3.4], dtype=StringDType())
L143:     array(['1', '<object object at 0x7faa2497dde0>', '3.4'], dtype=StringDType())
L144: If this behavior is not desired, an instance of the DType can be created that disables string coercion by setting `coerce=False` in the initializer:
L145: 
L146:     >>> np.array([1, object(), 3.4], dtype=StringDType(coerce=False))
L147:     Traceback (most recent call last):
L148:     ...
L149:     ValueError: StringDType only allows string data when string coercion is disabled.
L150: This allows strict data validation in the same pass over the data NumPy uses to create the array. Setting `coerce=True` recovers the default behavior allowing coercion to strings.
L151: ### Casting To and From Fixed-Width Strings【39†#】
L152: `StringDType` supports round-trip casts between 【28†`numpy.str_`】, 【29†`numpy.bytes_`】, and 【27†`numpy.void`】. Casting to a fixed-width string is most useful when strings need to be memory-mapped in an ndarray or when a fixed-width string is needed for reading and writing to a columnar data format with a known maximum string length.
L153: The 【29†`numpy.bytes_`】 cast is most useful for string data that is known to contain only ASCII characters, as characters outside this range cannot be represented in a single byte in the UTF-8 encoding and are rejected.
L154: When converting an array to a fixed-width string dtype with an unspecified size using 【40†`numpy.ndarray.astype`】, NumPy infers the size by inspecting the array values, producing a dtype wide enough to store the widest entry without truncation:
L155: 
L156:     >>> arr = np.array(["hello", "world!!"], dtype=StringDType())
L157:     >>> arr.astype(np.str_)
L158:     array(['hello', 'world!!'], dtype='<U7')
L159:     >>> arr.astype("S")
L160:     array([b'hello', b'world!!'], dtype='|S7')
L161: An explicit size can still be passed, truncating entries that do not fit:
L162: 
L163:     >>> arr.astype("U4")
L164:     array(['hell', 'worl'], dtype='<U4')
L165: 
L166: 
L167: Any valid unicode string can be cast to 【28†`numpy.str_`】, although since 【28†`numpy.str_`】 uses a 32-bit UCS4 encoding for all characters, this will often waste memory for real-world textual data that can be well-represented by a more memory-efficient encoding.
L168: Additionally, any valid unicode string can be cast to 【27†`numpy.void`】, storing the UTF-8 bytes directly in the output array:
L169: 
L170:     >>> arr = np.array(["hello", "world"], dtype=StringDType())
L171:     >>> arr.astype("V5")
L172:     array([b'\x68\x65\x6C\x6C\x6F', b'\x77\x6F\x72\x6C\x64'], dtype='|V5')
L173: Care must be taken to ensure that the output array has enough space for the UTF-8 bytes in the string, since the size of a UTF-8 bytestream in bytes is not necessarily the same as the number of characters in the string.
L174: 
L175: Conversions in the other direction, from a fixed-width string array to `StringDType` are `"safe"` casts. The bytes stored in a 【29†`numpy.bytes_`】 array must be valid UTF-8, and a `UnicodeDecodeError` is raised during the cast if they are not.
